ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A double pulley is free to rotate about its axis through its center. The radii of the two pulleys are $R$ and $2R$. Two cords are wrapped in opposite directions on the pulleys and are attached to masses. As a result, the two tension forces acting on the pulley are equal and acting downwards as shown in the image below so that $F_1 = 2F_2$. When released from rest, what will be the direction of the angular acceleration?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a coaxial double-radius pulley, with a rotation axle at the center. The radius of the inner smaller circle is labeled R, and the radius of the outer larger circle is labeled 2R. The rope on the left is wound around the wheel with inner radius R, and applies F1 vertically downward on the left side; the rope on the right is wound around the wheel with outer radius 2R, and applies F2 vertically downward on the right side. The two ropes are located on opposite sides, so the two downward pulling forces produce torques in opposite directions about the center. Reasoning: The left-side F1 acts at radius R, and the magnitude of the torque is tau1 = F1 R. The right-side F2 acts at radius 2R, and the magnitude of the torque is tau2 = F2(2R). The problem statement gives F1 = 2F2, so tau1 = (2F2)R = 2RF2, while tau2 = 2RF2. The two torques have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, so the net torque is zero. From sum tau = I alpha, it can be known that alpha = 0, so the pulley has no angular acceleration.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a compound pulley with a smaller inner drum of radius R carrying the left vertical downward force F1, and a larger outer drum of radius 2R carrying the right vertical downward force F2. The two cords are on opposite sides, so their torques about the center have opposite signs: the left downward F1 on radius R gives one rotational sense, while the right downward F2 on radius 2R gives the other. Compute magnitudes: tau1 = F1 R and tau2 = F2(2R). Use the text relation F1 = 2F2, so tau1 = (2F2)R = 2RF2 and tau2 = 2RF2. Since the torques are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, the net torque is zero; therefore by sum tau = I alpha, alpha = 0. The pulley has no angular acceleration.

method.method_draft: Use a virtual angular displacement argument. From the image, a small rotation of the pulley would unwind one cord while winding the other because the cords are wrapped in opposite directions: the left cord is on the small radius R and the right cord is on the large radius 2R. For a small angular displacement dtheta, the left cord end moves a length R dtheta, while the right cord end moves a length 2R dtheta in the opposite work sense. The generalized torque/work per angular displacement is therefore proportional to F1(R) - F2(2R), with signs opposite because the cords oppose each other. Insert the text relation F1 = 2F2: F1 R - 2RF2 = 2RF2 - 2RF2 = 0. Thus no net rotational work is available for either infinitesimal angular displacement, so the generalized torque is zero and the pulley cannot start angularly accelerating from rest.

A vertical cord on the left is tangent to the smaller pulley and has a downward force F1. A vertical cord on the right is tangent to the larger pulley and has a downward force F2. The two cords are wrapped in opposite directions around the pulleys.

Reasoning: Use a small virtual angular displacement dtheta. Because the cords are wrapped in opposite directions, one cord would unwind while the other winds, so their virtual work contributions have opposite signs. The left cord on radius R contributes F1 R dtheta in one rotational sense. The right cord on radius 2R contributes F2(2R)dtheta in the opposite rotational sense. Thus the generalized torque is proportional to F1 R - F2(2R). Given F1 = 2F2, this becomes (2F2)R - 2RF2 = 0. Therefore the net torque about the pulley axis is zero, so the pulley has no angular acceleration when released from rest.
